podcast: Dishing Up Digital with Ellen Mackenzie

fcb6a52807.q: What are the four key business moves to reach a first $10,000 per month milestone as a social media manager?
fcb6a52807.a: The four key levers are: prioritizing social proof through portfolios, case studies, and testimonials; shifting to premium pricing with retainers of $1,000 to $3,500 per month instead of hourly rates; implementing systems and software to streamline operations and free up time; and building a team or hiring contractors to support client delivery and allow time off. Ellen emphasizes that social proof must come first if you haven't hit $5,000 per month yet, then premium pricing becomes critical—with five clients at $2,000 per month being far more sustainable than twenty clients at $500 per month.

6cd411f802.q: Why is Q4 the best time of year for social media managers to reach their first $10,000 month?
6cd411f802.a: Q4 is a magical time because businesses are increasing their budgets and prioritizing social media more heavily, while consumers are getting out their wallets to purchase. This creates a ripple effect for social media managers and freelancers, as clients have more budget to spend on social services and are actively looking to capture holiday season spending.

ea80a5ba73.q: How many clients did Ellen Mackenzie manage to hit her first $10,000 month and what was the key hiring decision?
ea80a5ba73.a: Ellen was managing around eight different clients with various packages when she first hit $10,000, but she describes this approach as unsustainable and leading to burnout. The actual breakthrough came when she hired her first contractor—a former colleague—who worked just two hours per week on captions and client engagement. This small hire unlocked the $10,000 milestone after she had been stuck at $7,000 to $9,000 for months.

fdcf7e51c2.q: Should social media managers focus on posting content on social media before they have client experience and social proof?
fdcf7e51c2.a: No. Ellen emphasizes that new social media managers without client portfolios should focus on networking, co-pitching, and building experience first—not posting generic tips on social media. In her first 10 months as a freelancer, she did not post about her business on social media at all; she leveraged Facebook groups, attended networking events, and cold pitched instead. Only after building a portfolio of real client work should you begin posting social media content, because that is when you have case studies and results to share.
